It's hard to understand the issue unless you're a IQ120-cyborg. If you're new to linux I suggest you ignore it and install mint as you planned, systemd probably won't affect you in any meaningful way.

The core of the issue is that for a long time all the pieces of linux have been written with "do one thing and do it well" in mind, this is what has helped to make linux secure and stable. systemd throws that away and adopts a windows-like model of one package being a jack-of-all-trades gradually expanding and obliterating all the smaller system packages which have been reliable and stable for many years, some people are worried that this will introduce security problems.

If you have a little more experience you could try Devuan, basically its Debian but without systemd (I admit I haven't tried it yet so I have no idea how hard the install is). If you want to follow a steep learning curve and become one of the "cyborgs" then you could try Gentoo which can be installed with or without systemd.

This really is what makes sense.

The super simple version is that with the old systems like initd you have a screwdriver.. Its only a screwdriver, but damn, it is a freaking good screwdriver.

In the new systemd world... Its a piece of a screwdriver that is integrated into other tools that share common uses. Sadly, that means that a good screwdriver can also be a crappy hammer. That is systemd. (mr. multi-tool)

However, This is the new world of enterprise Linux. If you are not going to run these systems in a business world. Who cares, use what you like. If you want to be a sysadmin in enterprise. Lear systemd (and RedHat/Fedora).
Don't skip Linux, just use Devuan instead.
